title: OpenAI Pays $3.2 Million to Settle U.S. Claims It Favored Foreign Visa Workers
excerpt: The DOJ alleged ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and subsidiary Statsig discriminated against American job applicants through the Permanent Labor Certification process, making it the highest-profile company to settle in the Trump administration's crackdown on visa program abuse.
body:
• OpenAI and subsidiary Statsig will pay $3.2 million — $1.2 million in civil penalties and $2 million to compensate victims — to settle DOJ discrimination claims.
  • The DOJ alleged OpenAI discouraged U.S. workers by requiring paper applications, not posting jobs publicly, and airing radio ads late at night.
  • Fewer than 10 positions were at issue, but the DOJ said the settlement size reflects the harm to workers shut out of lucrative tech jobs.
  • OpenAI denied wrongdoing but agreed to revise hiring policies, conduct anti-discrimination training, and submit to DOJ monitoring.

OpenAI and its subsidiary Statsig Inc. will pay $3.2 million to settle U.S. Justice Department allegations that they discriminated against American job applicants by favoring foreign workers on temporary employment visas, the DOJ announced on Tuesday. The settlement marks the highest-profile enforcement action since the Trump administration relaunched its crackdown on alleged abuse of foreign worker visa programs last year.

The DOJ's Civil Rights Division alleged that both companies violated the Immigration and Nationality Act, which prohibits discrimination based on citizenship status, through their use of the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) process — a pathway that allows employers to sponsor foreign workers for permanent residency after demonstrating a good-faith effort to recruit qualified American workers first.

What the DOJ Found

Federal investigators concluded that OpenAI took multiple steps to discourage U.S. workers from applying for positions it sought to fill through the PERM program. According to the DOJ, the San Francisco-based AI company failed to advertise PERM positions on its external careers website, even though standard practice for other openings was to post them publicly. OpenAI also required applicants for these roles to submit paper applications by mail, while accepting electronic applications for all other positions.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=9cKRJJL4SPY

In some cases, the company aired radio advertisements for these jobs late at night — a tactic the DOJ said further limited the pool of American applicants who would see the openings, according to Reuters. Statsig, a Bellevue, Washington-based product development software company and OpenAI subsidiary, was also named in the investigation.

"It is illegal to discriminate against U.S. workers by preferring temporary visa holders for jobs. This substantial settlement ensures that OpenAI redresses harm and changes its recruitment practices so that U.S. workers receive a fair opportunity for highly sought-after technology positions."

— Harmeet Dhillon, Assistant Attorney General, DOJ Civil Rights Division

Settlement Terms

The $3.2 million settlement breaks down into $1.2 million in civil penalties paid to the U.S. government and a $2 million fund to compensate individuals the DOJ identified as victims of discriminatory hiring practices. While fewer than 10 positions were at issue, the DOJ said the sizeable amount reflected the harm caused when U.S. workers are "shut out of applying for lucrative technology jobs," according to the Wall Street Journal.

Beyond the financial penalties, OpenAI agreed to revise its employment policies to ensure PERM positions are posted on its public career website and that electronic applications are accepted. The company must also conduct anti-discrimination training for relevant personnel and submit to ongoing Justice Department monitoring.

An OpenAI spokesman told the Wall Street Journal the company disagreed with the DOJ's findings but reached a settlement to resolve the matter, adding that the PERM program is "critical for employees and candidates requiring immigration support." The company denied wrongdoing in the settlement agreement.

Part of a Broader Crackdown

The OpenAI settlement is the latest — and most prominent — in a series of enforcement actions targeting tech companies over alleged visa program abuse. The DOJ has announced at least a dozen similar settlements since last year, but none involving a company as high-profile as the maker of ChatGPT.

The action fits within the Trump administration's broader push to limit foreign worker hiring. President Trump has argued that many companies exploit the temporary employment visa system and last year proposed imposing a $100,000 fee on new H-1B visas for highly skilled workers — up from roughly $5,000. That fee increase, which sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley, was blocked by an appeals court in June and remains tied up in legal challenges.

What It Means for the Indian Tech Workforce

The settlement carries particular weight for the Indian diaspora, which accounts for the largest share of H-1B visa holders in the United States. Indian tech workers have long relied on the PERM process as a critical step toward obtaining green cards, and any enforcement actions or policy shifts around the program directly affect their career trajectories.

The case also highlights the tension between the tech industry's dependence on global talent — particularly from India — and the current administration's efforts to prioritize American workers. Earlier this year, OpenAI pledged to cover legal costs and provide support for employees facing immigration enforcement actions, reflecting the precarious position many foreign-born tech workers navigate daily.

What's Next

The DOJ's Civil Rights Division is expected to continue pursuing similar cases against other tech companies. For OpenAI, the settlement closes one chapter but opens another: the company will operate under federal monitoring as it overhauls its recruitment practices. With the H-1B fee proposal still pending in the courts and immigration enforcement intensifying, the broader landscape for foreign tech workers in the U.S. remains in flux.
